title: The Coinbase allegations expose Bitcoin's corporate governance gap
summary: Corporate adoption of bitcoin will stall as long as companies can't show who controls the money, who approves its movement, or whether it's still there, says Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma.
gpt_reference_summary: BlockTower founder Ari Paul accused Coinbase of losing about $25 million of his firm's assets and hiding more than $1 billion in hacks affecting institutions, allegations Coinbase denies. In this opinion column, Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma argues that the dispute exposes companies' difficulty independently checking their bitcoin holdings and who can move them. He advocates systems requiring approval from multiple independent institutions, clear staff permissions and records of withdrawals.
gemini_reference_summary: In an opinion column, Onramp CEO Michael Tanguma argues that BlockTower Capital founder Ari Paul's disputed accusation that Coinbase lost $25 million of his firm's funds and hid over $1 billion in institutional hacks highlights a major weakness in how companies store Bitcoin. Because neither side's claims can be independently verified by outsiders, Tanguma contends that storing corporate Bitcoin under a single exchange login or individual hardware device lacks the basic oversight, staff permissions, and audit trails that corporate boards require for bank accounts. To fix this, he advocates using Bitcoin's built-in multi-signature technology, which distributes security keys across multiple independent institutions so no single party can move or lose the funds alone.

title: OCC's final rule to start fresh in weighing stablecoin rewards against GENIUS Act ban
summary: The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is the first of several federal agencies to finish writing regulations under the act.
gpt_reference_summary: The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a final rule under the GENIUS Act governing stablecoins, digital currencies designed to track the dollar, scheduled to take effect on January 18. It will assess rewards programs individually against the law's ban on issuers paying customers solely for holding or using stablecoins, without automatically approving programs that already exist. Other federal agencies are still writing related rules, leaving parts of the law's implementation unfinished.
gemini_reference_summary: The U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which regulates national banks, issued the first final rule implementing the GENIUS Act, a federal law governing dollar-pegged digital currencies known as stablecoins, set to take effect on January 18. Under the rule, cryptocurrency exchanges like Coinbase, PayPal, and Kraken will not get automatic approval for their existing customer rewards programs and must have them reviewed case by case against the law's ban on paying interest solely for holding a stablecoin. While the OCC finalized its rules for issuing and safeguarding stablecoins, other federal agencies including the Federal Reserve, the Treasury Department, and the FDIC are still writing their portions of the regulations.

title: Crypto Long & Short: Why real-world assets need fixed-rate loans onchain
summary: Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners explains why fixed-rate, fixed-term lending is the missing piece, and how a 5% shift in Sky and Ethena reserves could create $1.8 billion of demand for real-world assets.
gpt_reference_summary: Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners argues that loans with fixed interest rates and repayment dates are needed to expand borrowing against stocks, bonds and other real-world assets represented on cryptocurrency networks. He says current loans with changing rates can become more expensive than the income those assets earn, while borrowers may have to wait to sell or redeem them. As a hypothetical example, he estimates that shifting 5% of Sky and Ethena's reserves into strategies using borrowed money could generate $1.8 billion in demand for such assets.
gemini_reference_summary: In an analysis for CoinDesk's Crypto Long & Short newsletter, Peter Gaffney of O2O Capital Partners argues that blockchain lending platforms need loans with fixed interest rates and set repayment dates to expand borrowing against tokenized real-world assets like bonds and credit funds. Currently, most blockchain loans use fluctuating interest rates that can suddenly spike above the 4.5% to 5.2% annual returns those traditional assets pay, trapping borrowers whose underlying investments can take weeks or months to cash out. Gaffney estimates that moving just 5% of the $12 billion in reserves held by stablecoin projects Sky and Ethena into fixed-rate borrowing strategies could generate $1.8 billion in new demand for tokenized real-world assets.

gpt_reference_summary: Robinhood executive JB Mackenzie said contracts letting customers bet on bitcoin, gold and oil prices are among its fastest-growing prediction-market products, although sports remains its largest category. These contracts pay according to whether an event happens, such as bitcoin exceeding a set price, without requiring users to buy the asset. The Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision was Robinhood's biggest event contract in September, and some cryptocurrency contracts now settle in just 15 minutes.
gemini_reference_summary: Trading app Robinhood is seeing rapid growth in prediction markets—contracts that let users bet yes or no on future events without buying the underlying asset—tied to the prices of Bitcoin, gold, and crude oil, according to company executive JB Mackenzie. Although sports betting remains Robinhood's largest prediction-market category, its single biggest event contract in September was tied to the U.S. Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision, and some cryptocurrency price contracts now settle in as little as 15 minutes. Mackenzie added that these short-term event contracts, offered through a partnership with regulated exchange Kalshi, are also drawing new customers into Robinhood's stock, cryptocurrency, options, and retirement accounts.

title: Bitcoin Core changes security rules as AI makes finding code bugs dangerously easy
summary: Developers merged a policy change that ends the months-long embargo for bugs a chatbot could rediscover, after a summer in which AI found hundreds of bitcoin bugs before the humans did.
gpt_reference_summary: Bitcoin Core developers changed their security policy to release fixes and disclose details quickly when a software flaw can be rediscovered with a simple AI request. The change replaces delays that could last months, aiming to protect users sooner, although developers acknowledge that fixes may receive less testing before release. No vulnerability has yet been designated under the new rule.
gemini_reference_summary: Developers of Bitcoin Core, the main software used to run the Bitcoin network, updated their security policy on Thursday to quickly patch and publicly disclose software bugs that can be easily discovered using a simple prompt to an artificial intelligence chatbot. Previously, developers kept medium- and high-risk flaws secret for months after quietly releasing fixes so computer operators had time to upgrade, but the rapid rise of AI tools—including a July test where AI flagged nearly 5,000 potential flaws across 390 Bitcoin projects in a single day—made it too easy for attackers to uncover hidden bugs on their own. While developer Antoine Poinsot acknowledged that rushing out fixes means updates will get less testing time before reaching users, maintainers concluded that long secrecy periods no longer protect the network against easily rediscovered flaws.

title: Bitcoin's price is as jumpy as Nvidia's and eight times more turbulent than the euro
summary: Your day-ahead look for Oct. 23, 2026 This is an excerpt from CoinDesk newsletter 'Daybook.' Sign up here, if you haven't already.
gpt_reference_summary: CoinDesk's comparison of daily price changes over 90 days found bitcoin's price about as jumpy as Nvidia shares, with swings more than three times those of the S&P 500 stock index and about eight times those of the euro against the dollar. Bitcoin's price swings have declined compared with their average since 2020, but remain larger than those of gold and major national currencies.
gemini_reference_summary: Although Bitcoin's price swings have calmed down compared with its historical average since 2020, a CoinDesk analysis of 90-day price movements shows the cryptocurrency remains far more volatile than traditional currencies, gold, and the broader stock market. As of Thursday, Bitcoin's 90-day volatility gauge stood at about 38%—nearly identical to artificial intelligence chipmaker Nvidia at 37%—making it more than three times as jumpy as the S&P 500 stock index (11%), rougher than gold (23.5%), and about eight times as turbulent as the euro-to-U.S.-dollar exchange rate (4.6%). The comparison shows that while Bitcoin now trades much like a major technology stock, its price is still too unstable to match national currencies used for everyday payments.

title: Live updates: Bitcoin holds above $81,000 as oil prices hit six-month high
summary: Yesterday’s 19 basis point slide in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was the largest one-day move downward since March 2023, when the failure of Silicon Valley Bank had investors worried about a domino effect across the country.
gpt_reference_summary: Bitcoin steadied near $81,500 on Friday after large swings earlier in the week, while U.S. stock markets were broadly flat. Brent oil reached its highest level since early May, complicating the inflation outlook before the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting.
gemini_reference_summary: Bitcoin steadied near $81,500 on Friday after a turbulent week of $3,000 price swings, even as U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds suffered $635 million in investor withdrawals on Thursday—their largest single-day outflow since June 25, according to Farside Investors. Data from Farside shows that after the 22 previous occasions when daily fund withdrawals topped $300 million, Bitcoin's price was significantly lower on average 7, 30, and 90 days later, though analysts note the funds have less than three years of trading history. Meanwhile, U.S. stock markets held mostly flat, gold dipped below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since July, and Brent crude oil hit its highest level since early May ahead of next week's Federal Reserve interest-rate meeting.

title: Bitcoin appears to have decoupled from midterm cycle bottom history
summary: Previous bitcoin bear-market lows followed U.S. midterms, but this year’s recovery raises the possibility that the bottom arrived months earlier.
gpt_reference_summary: Bitcoin's recovery has raised the possibility that this year's lowest price came before the U.S. midterm elections, unlike major lows following the 2014, 2018 and 2022 elections. It rose about 40% from $57,850 on July 1 to roughly $81,455 on October 22, with the July low occurring 125 days before Election Day. The article suggests the historical pattern is linked more closely to bitcoin's own market cycles than to the elections themselves.
gemini_reference_summary: With U.S. midterm elections 10 days away, Bitcoin's 40% recovery from its July 1 low of $57,850 to around $81,455 on October 22 suggests its current market cycle may have hit bottom months earlier than in past midterm election years. In the 2014, 2018, and 2022 midterm cycles, Bitcoin reached its lowest downturn price 71, 38, and 13 days after Election Day, whereas this year's low arrived 125 days before the November 3 vote. Comparing Bitcoin's price history with the tech-heavy Invesco QQQ stock fund—which fell around the 2018 and 2022 midterms but rose before the 2014 vote—indicates that Bitcoin's past downturns around midterm elections were driven more by its own internal market cycles than by politics.

title: Sweden’s central bank revives e-krona debate as stablecoins and digital euro loom
summary: Sweden’s central bank warns foreign stablecoins and a digital euro risk eroding krona demand.
gpt_reference_summary: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, wants lawmakers to reconsider an e-krona, a digital form of money issued directly by the central bank for public use. It warns that foreign-currency stablecoins and a planned digital euro could reduce use of the Swedish krona and weaken its control over the economy and national payments. The bank has not decided whether to issue an e-krona, and preparing a launch would take at least five years.
gemini_reference_summary: Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, is urging lawmakers to reconsider creating a digital version of the national currency, called an e-krona, warning that foreign-currency stablecoins and a planned digital euro could weaken the Swedish krona's role in everyday payments. With survey data showing only 5% of Swedes used physical cash for their last purchase, central bank officials say a public digital krona would help maintain control over the national economy and provide an offline backup payment system during power or telecommunications outages. Although a 2023 government inquiry found little immediate need for an e-krona and the Riksbank has not yet decided whether to issue one, the bank wants legal preparations to begin now because building and launching the system would take at least five years.
